name: Executive order of July 30, 1869 accepting Fort Hall as the Bannock reservation of the Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868
citation: Executive Order of July 30, 1869, under the Treaty with the Eastern Band Shoshoni and Bannock of July 3, 1868 (15 Stat. 673)
promises: Royce records that the treaty of July 3, 1868 authorized the President to set apart a reserve for the Bannock whenever they wished, and that by this order the Fort Hall reserve was accepted as the reserve the treaty contemplated.
The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes state the Fort Hall Reservation was set aside by executive order as the Bannock reservation guaranteed in the Fort Bridger Treaty.

breaches.what: The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes state that the Fort Hall Reservation originally contained 1.8 million acres, that this was reduced to 1.2 million acres in 1872 because of a survey error, and that later legislation and allotment reduced it to its present size.

A claim that the United States failed to provide the Bannock the reservation promised by the treaty of July 3, 1868 (Docket 326-G, also raised in Docket 366) was settled, with six other Shoshone and Bannock claims, by one consolidated final judgment of $15,700,000, without a trial of that claim.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Dockets 326-D to 326-H, 366 and 367, compromise settlement

source.title: Shoshone-Bannock Tribes et al. v. United States, Dockets 326-D to 326-H, 366 and 367, Findings of Fact on Settlement (19 Ind. Cl. Comm. 3, February 13, 1968)
source.publisher: Indian Claims Commission Decisions, Oklahoma State University Library

compensation: A compromise of $15,700,000 in 1968 settled seven dockets together, including the Bannock reservation claim; no amount was assigned to it alone.
today: The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes state the reservation lies north and west of Pocatello, Idaho, reduced to its present size by legislation and allotment.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribes say the Fort Hall Reservation was set aside by executive order as the Bannock reservation guaranteed in the Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868, that it first held 1.8 million acres, that a survey error cut it to 1.2 million acres in 1872, and that later legislation and allotment reduced it further.

openQuestions: Royce area 524 is the Fort Hall reserve, not a cession; the two Royce records dated June 14, 1867 and July 30, 1869 both point to it.

treaties.json names the Coeur d'Alene among the scheduleTribes for Royce 524. Royce's schedule also mentions an original reserve established by executive order of June 14, 1867 in its Washington and Idaho notes; whether that is the Coeur d'Alene reserve was not settled, and the Coeur d'Alene are not parties to Fort Hall.
No Commission or court finding on the 1872 survey reduction was located; the claims about the 1888-89 and 1898 cessions of reservation land (Dockets 326-E and 326-F) were settled without trial.
The text of the 1867 and 1869 executive orders was not opened; their terms are taken from Royce.
The Fort Bridger Treaty of 1868 itself has its own record; this file covers only the 1869 order that named Fort Hall as the Bannock reserve.

plain.promised: The 1868 Fort Bridger Treaty promised the Bannock a reservation. In 1869 the President named the Fort Hall Reservation as that reserve.
plain.happened: The Shoshone-Bannock Tribes say a survey error cut Fort Hall from 1.8 to 1.2 million acres in 1872. A claim that the Bannock never got their promised reservation was settled, not decided.
plain.today: That claim was settled with six others for $15,700,000 in 1968, without a finding.
